facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus lived during the Lower Hettangian to Toarcian stages.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Lower Hettangian-Toarcian

facts.statement: The first known fossil of Temnodontosaurus was a complete skull and partial skeleton found by Joseph and Mary Anning in the early 1810s in Dorset, England.
facts.quote: The first known fossil is a specimen consisting of a complete skull and partial skeleton discovered on a cliff by Joseph and Mary Anning around the early 1810s in Dorset, England.

facts.statement: Sir Everard Home analyzed the first Temnodontosaurus specimen between 1814 and 1819, making it the first ichthyosaur to be scientifically described.
facts.quote: The anatomy of this specimen was subsequently analyzed in a series of articles written by Sir Everard Home between 1814 and 1819, making it the very first ichthyosaur to have been scientifically described.

facts.statement: William Conybeare assigned the first Temnodontosaurus specimen to the species Ichthyosaurus platyodon in 1822.
facts.quote: In 1822, the specimen was assigned to the genus Ichthyosaurus by William Conybeare, and more precisely to the species I. platyodon.

facts.statement: Richard Lydekker proposed the genus name Temnodontosaurus in 1889 due to large dental differences with other Ichthyosaurus species.
facts.quote: Noting the large dental differences with other species of Ichthyosaurus, Richard Lydekker suggested in 1889 moving this species into a separate genus, which he named Temnodontosaurus.

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus is generally estimated to be 9 meters long, making it one of the largest known ichthyosaurs.
facts.quote: Generally estimated at 9 m long, Temnodontosaurus is one of the largest known ichthyosaurs, although not as imposing as some Triassic forms.

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus had eye sockets wider than 25 cm, possibly giving it the largest eyes in the animal kingdom.
facts.quote: Boasting eye sockets measuring more than 25 cm wide, Temnodontosaurus quite possibly had the largest eyes known in the entire animal kingdom, rivaling in size those of the colossal squid.

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus had a snout longer than its lower jaw equipped with sharp teeth.
facts.quote: The snout appears to be longer than the mandible, being equipped with several sharp teeth (hence its name).

facts.statement: Based on complete skeletons, Temnodontosaurus is estimated to have had more than 40 presacral vertebrae.
facts.quote: On the basis of numerous very complete skeletons, it is estimated that the animal had at least more than 40 presacral vertebrae.

facts.statement: The family Temnodontosauridae was established in 1974 to include the genus Temnodontosaurus.
facts.quote: A monotypic family, Temnodontosauridae, was even established in 1974 to include the genus.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analyses suggest Temnodontosaurus is currently a polyphyletic taxon and requires revision.
facts.quote: Various phylogenetic analyses as well as diagnostic problems concerning the genus make it, for the moment, a polyphyletic taxon (unnatural grouping), and therefore in need of revision.

facts.statement: Joseph Anning discovered the first skull of Temnodontosaurus around 1810 on the cliffs of Black Ven in Dorset, England.
facts.quote: Around 1810, a certain Joseph Anning discovered the first skull of the taxon on the cliffs of Black Ven, between the town of Lyme Regis and the village of Charmouth, two localities located in the county of Dorset, in the south of England.

facts.statement: Mary Anning discovered the remaining skeleton of the first Temnodontosaurus specimen in 1812.
facts.quote: The remaining skeleton was later discovered by his sister, the now famous Mary Anning, in 1812.

facts.statement: William Bullock sold his collection containing the Temnodontosaurus specimen to the Natural History Museum in London for around £47 in 1819.
facts.quote: In 1819, Bullock's own collection was sold to the Natural History Museum in London for a price of around £47.

facts.statement: The primary Temnodontosaurus specimen is cataloged as NHMUK PV R 1158 and is housed at the Natural History Museum in London, though its postcranial remains are lost.
facts.quote: The specimen, now cataloged as NHMUK PV R 1158, is still currently housed at this museum, although the postcranial remains have since been lost.

facts.statement: Sir Everard Home initially classified the Temnodontosaurus fossil as an intermediate form between salamanders and lizards and named the genus Proteosaurus in 1819.
facts.quote: In 1819, he thought that the fossil represented an animal that embodied an intermediate form between salamanders and lizards, which led him to erect the genus name Proteosaurus (originally written as Proteo-Saurus).

facts.statement: Henry De la Beche named the species Ichthyosaurus platyodon in 1822 based on anatomical differences.
facts.quote: It was in 1822 that De la Beche named three species of Ichthyosaurus on the basis of several anatomical differences distinguishing the specimens, one of them being I. platyodon.

facts.statement: The species name platyodon refers to the flat teeth of the animal, derived from Ancient Greek words for flat and tooth.
facts.quote: The specific name platyodon comes from the Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, "flat", "broad"), and ὀδούς (odoús, "tooth"), all meaning "flat teeth", in reference to the rather distinctive dentition of this species.

facts.statement: Henry Alleyne Nicholson and Richard Lydekker published a detailed work on prehistoric vertebrates in 1889.
facts.quote: In 1889, Henry Alleyne Nicholson and Richard Lydekker published a two-volume work that served as an introduction to the rules of paleontology for students.

facts.statement: Christopher McGowan designated specimen NHMUK PV OR 2003* as the neotype for Temnodontosaurus after the original holotype tooth was lost in 1960.
facts.quote: As the latter has since been noted as lost in 1960, McGowan designated specimen NHMUK PV OR 2003* as the neotype of this taxon.

facts.statement: The neotype specimen of Temnodontosaurus was discovered and partly collected by Mary Anning in July 1832 in Lyme Regis.
facts.quote: This specimen, already mentioned as a representative of the species by Richard Owen in 1881, was originally discovered and partly collected by Mary Anning in July 1832 in Lyme Regis.

facts.statement: Mary Anning sold the neotype specimen to Thomas Hawkins, who then sold it to the Natural History Museum in London in 1834 for £210.
facts.quote: After the discovery, she sold the find to Thomas Hawkins, who himself sold the specimen to the Natural History Museum in London in 1834 for a price of £210.

facts.statement: The type species of Temnodontosaurus is Ichthyosaurus platyodon.
facts.quote: type_species: Ichthyosaurus platyodon

facts.statement: Recognized species of Temnodontosaurus include T. trigonodon, T. crassimanus, T. zetlandicus, and T. nuertingensis.
facts.quote: subdivision: Recognized species † T. trigonodon (von Theodori, 1843) † T. crassimanus (Blake, 1876) † T. zetlandicus (Seeley, 1876) † T. nuertingensis (von Huene, 1931)

facts.statement: The species T. eurycephalus and T. azerguensis are considered disputed within the genus Temnodontosaurus.
facts.quote: Disputed species † T.? eurycephalus McGowan, 1974 † T.? azerguensis Martin et al., 2012

facts.statement: Carl von Theodori described the species I. trigonodon in 1843 based on a colossal specimen found in Holzmaden, Baden-Württemberg, Germany.
facts.quote: In 1843, Carl von Theodori described a new species of Ichthyosaurus, I. trigonodon, which he described as "colossal", based on an imposing specimen comprising a complete skull and a partial postcranial skeleton discovered in the town of Holzmaden in the state of Baden-Württemberg, Germany.

facts.statement: The specific name trigonodon refers to the visibly triangular shape of the dental crown.
facts.quote: The specific name comes from Ancient Greek τρίγωνον (trígônon, "triangle") and ὀδούς (odoús, "tooth"), in reference to the dental crown which is visibly triangular in this species.

facts.statement: Friedrich von Huene transferred the species to the genus Leptopterygius in 1931.
facts.quote: In 1931, Friedrich von Huene transferred this species to the genus Leptopterygius.

facts.statement: Michael W. Maisch moved the species back to the genus Temnodontosaurus in 1998, including specimens from Germany and France.
facts.quote: In 1998, Michael W. Maisch moved the species again to the genus Temnodontosaurus, and attributed to this taxon other, mostly very complete, specimens having been discovered in Germany and France.

facts.statement: Owen classified the specimen as a new species named I. crassimanus in 1858.
facts.quote: The following year, 1858, Owen examined the specimen and classified it as distinct from I. platyodon, attributing it to a completely new species which he named I. crassimanus.

facts.statement: McGowan and Motani suggested in 2003 that specimens attributed to I. crassimanus belong to a distinct species of Temnodontosaurus, renamed T. crassimanus.
facts.quote: In 2003, McGowan and Ryosuke Motani suggested that all specimens historically attributed to I. crassimanus appeared sufficiently different from T. platyodon and T. trigonodon to belong to a distinct species of the genus Temnodontosaurus, being renamed T. crassimanus.

facts.statement: McGowan and Motani noted that further research could question the validity of T. crassimanus.
facts.quote: However, they note that further research could question its validity.

facts.statement: Harry Govier Seeley described the species I. zetlandicus in 1880 based on a skull loaned by an Earl of Shetland.
facts.quote: In 1880, Harry Govier Seeley described the species I. zetlandicus on the basis of a well-preserved skull loaned by an Earl of Shetland (hence its name) around an unspecified date to the Sedgwick Museum of Earth Sciences in Cambridge.

facts.statement: Antoine Laboury and colleagues attributed a partial skull discovered in Schouweiler, southern Luxembourg, to the taxon.
facts.quote: In their description, they attribute another specimen to the taxon, cataloged as MNHNL TU885, a partial skull which was originally discovered in Schouweiler, southern Luxembourg.

facts.statement: Friedrich von Huene described the species L. nürtingensis in 1931 based on a specimen discovered in a quarry in Nürtingen, Baden-Württemberg, Germany.
facts.quote: In 1931, von Huene described a new species of the genus Leptopterygius, L. nürtingensis, based on a skull and some postcranial remains of a single specimen discovered in a quarry in the town of Nürtingen (hence its name), Baden-Württemberg, Germany.

facts.statement: Oskar Kuhn assimilated an incomplete specimen from Aue-Fallstein, Lower Saxony, to the species in 1939, but the specimen is now viewed as indeterminate due to lack of evidence.
facts.quote: In 1939, Oskar Kuhn assimilated an incomplete specimen discovered in Aue-Fallstein, Lower Saxony, to this species. However, Kuhn did not present sufficient evidence to confirm his claims, and the specimen has since been viewed as indeterminate.

facts.statement: Maisch and Hungerbühler considered the holotype specimen attributable to Temnodontosaurus in 1997 after redescribing it.
facts.quote: In 1997, Maisch and Axel Hungerbühler formally criticized McGowan's view, given that the holotype specimen is preserved in an excellent state of conservation and is easily diagnosable. He then redescribed this specimen and considered it to be attributable to Temnodontosaurus.

facts.statement: McGowan and Motani considered the species a nomen dubium in 2003, but its validity and genus assignment are maintained in subsequent studies.
facts.quote: The species is again considered a nomen dubium by McGowan and Motani in 2003, but its validity as well as its belonging to this genus is maintained in subsequent studies.

facts.statement: The specific name azerguensis comes from the Azergues river near the discovery site.
facts.quote: The specific name comes from the Azergues, a river located near the site of the discovery.

facts.statement: McGowan redescribed the large skull from Lyme Regis and made it the holotype of the new species T. eurycephalus.
facts.quote: Although I. breviceps is still recognized as belonging to this genus, the large skull historically attributed to the species has large differences with the holotype specimen. Noting this, McGowan redescribed this specimen in more detail and made it the holotype of an entirely new species of Temnodontosaurus, T. eurycephalus.

facts.statement: Richard Owen named the species I. acutirostris in 1840 based on a partial skeleton found near Whitby.
facts.quote: In 1840, Owen named the species I. acutirostris on the basis of a partial skeleton discovered near Whitby, now numbered NHMUK PV OR 14553.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of I. acutirostris was officially found in 2002 after being considered lost for a long time, though parts like the snout are missing.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen was for a long time noted as lost, but this was only in 2002 when it was officially found, although some anatomical parts such as the snout are missing.

facts.statement: In 2022, Laboury and colleagues concluded that I. acutirostris should be considered a species inquirenda.
facts.quote: In 2022, Laboury and colleagues share the same conclusions and considers "I." acutirostris as a species inquirenda.

facts.statement: Albert Gaudry officially described the species I. burgundiae in 1892 based on a specimen found in the quarries of Sainte-Colombe, Yonne, France.
facts.quote: In 1892, Albert Gaudry officially described a new species of Ichthyosaurus, I. burgundiae, on the basis of a specimen discovered in the quarries of the town of Sainte-Colombe, in Yonne, France.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of I. burgundiae was donated to the National Museum of Natural History in Paris on November 12, 1889, and remains exhibited there today.
facts.quote: After the end of the exhibition, the specimen was subsequently donated to the National Museum of Natural History in Paris, joining its collection on November 12, 1889, where it is still exhibited to this day.

facts.statement: In 1998, Maisch suggested synonymizing T. burgundiae with T. trigonodon based on a comparison with the holotype.
facts.quote: In 1998, Maisch compared these specimens to the holotype of T. trigonodon, and suggested synonymizing T. burgundiae with the latter.

facts.statement: McGowan described the species T. risor in 1974 based on three skulls found at Lyme Regis, designating NHMUK PV R43971 as the holotype.
facts.quote: In 1974, McGowan described an additional species of Temnodontosaurus, T. risor, based on three skulls discovered at Lyme Regis, designating NHMUK PV R43971 as the holotype specimen.

facts.statement: McGowan distinguished T. risor from other species based on larger orbits, smaller maxillae, and a curved snout.
facts.quote: In his description, he justifies the distinction of this species via the larger orbits, the smaller maxillae and the curved snout.

facts.statement: In 1995, McGowan revised his earlier work and found that the three specimens attributed to T. risor were actually juveniles of T. platyodon, with previous distinctions being growth stages.
facts.quote: In 1995, the same author carried out a more in-depth revision of the three specimens attributed to this taxon. He then discovered that the characteristics he had previously judged to be distinctive were in fact stages of growth, the three specimens representing juveniles of T. platyodon.

facts.statement: While the full body color of Temnodontosaurus is unknown, a T. trigonodon specimen showed dark coloration on its forefins, similar to other early ichthyosaurs with preserved eumelanin pigments.
facts.quote: Although the full body colour of Temnodontosaurus is unknown, at least some ichthyosaurs may have been uniformly dark-coloured in life, which is evidenced by the discovery of high concentrations of eumelanin pigments in the preserved skin of an early ichthyosaur fossil, and a specimen of T. trigonodon had similarly dark coloration on at least the forefins.

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus is one of the largest ichthyosaurs known, though it is not as large as Triassic forms like Shonisaurus or Ichthyotitan.
facts.quote: Temnodontosaurus is one of the largest ichthyosaurs identified to date, although the species which belong to it are not as imposing as Triassic forms like Shonisaurus, Himalayasaurus, Cymbospondylus or Ichthyotitan.

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus represents the largest known ichthyosaur within the parvipelvian group.
facts.quote: It nevertheless represents the largest known ichthyosaur of the parvipelvian group.

facts.statement: Specimens of T. platyodon, T. trigonodon, and T. crassimanus have been estimated to reach a body length of around 9 meters.
facts.quote: Based on different specimens, the species T. platyodon, T. trigonodon and T. crassimanus have body sizes estimated to be around 9 m in length.

facts.statement: The incomplete holotype specimen of T. crassimanus suggests a skull length of approximately 1 meter.
facts.quote: Although incomplete, the holotype specimen of T. crassimanus would have had a skull estimated to be around 1 m long.

facts.statement: T. zetlandicus and T. nuertingensis lack body length estimates, but their skull sizes of 1 to 1.3 meters suggest they are smaller than other Temnodontosaurus species.
facts.quote: No body length estimates for T. zetlandicus and T. nuertingensis have currently been given. However, the measurement of their skull, reaching respectively 1 to 1.3 m in length, suggests that they are smaller representatives when compared to the three species previously mentioned.

facts.statement: An estimate of 16 meters for a Temnodontosaurus specimen based on vertebrae from Banz Abbey Museum was later found to be exaggerated because the reference skeleton used was shorter than assumed.
facts.quote: In 1996, McGowan nominally assigned the specimen to Temnodontosaurus, although without specific assignment. Based on SMNS 50000, a nearly complete skeleton of T. trigonodon, the author estimated the size of Banz's specimen at 16 m long, as Huene initially suggested. However, this estimate turned out to be exaggerated, as specimen SMNS 50000 is shorter than what had been assumed during the formulation of the estimate.

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus had forefins and hindfins of roughly equal length that were narrow and elongated.
facts.quote: The forefins and hindfins of Temnodontosaurus were of roughly the same length and were rather narrow and elongated.

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus possessed an unreduced, tripartite pelvic girdle and had three primary digits plus one postaxial accessory digit.
facts.quote: Furthermore, the genus differed from ichthyosaurs such as Ichthyosaurus in possessing an unreduced, tripartite pelvic girdle and having only three primary digits with one postaxial accessory digit.

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus had a tail with a weak bend of less than 35 degrees, and its caudal fin has been described as either lunate or semi-lunate.
facts.quote: Although it had a weak tail bend at an angle of less than 35°; its caudal fin has variously been described as either lunate or semi-lunate.

facts.statement: The caudal fin of Temnodontosaurus consisted of two lobes, with the lower lobe supported by vertebrae and the upper lobe lacking bony support.
facts.quote: This fin was made of two lobes, in which the lower lobe was skeletally supported by vertebrae whereas the upper lobe had no bony support.

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus had fewer than 90 vertebrae, with the vertebral axis and atlas fused to aid in stabilization during swimming.
facts.quote: It had roughly less than 90 vertebrae, and the vertebral axis and atlas were fused together, serving as stabilization during swimming.

facts.statement: Preserved eumelanin and evenly spaced stripes were found on the forefin, and the fin tip likely acted as a flexible winglet.
facts.quote: Preserved eumelanin (pigments responsible for black layer of skin) and "evenly spaced stripes" are also present across the forefin, and the tip of the fin likely acted as a "flexible winglet".

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus had many pointed conical teeth set in continuous grooves rather than individual sockets, a condition known as aulacodonty.
facts.quote: It also had many pointed conical teeth that were set in continuous grooves, rather than having individual sockets. This form of tooth implantation is known as aulacodonty.

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus was a genus of ichthyosaurs from the Early Jurassic, living between 198 and 185 million years ago in what is now Europe (England and Germany).
facts.quote: Temnodontosaurus es un género de ictiosaurios del Jurásico Inferior, viviendo entre 198 a 185 millones de años (Hettangiense - Toarciense), en lo que hoy es Europa (Inglaterra y Alemania).

facts.statement: Species of Temnodontosaurus were large animals, reaching up to 12 meters in length, with great muscular strength and were skilled coastal predators.
facts.quote: Las especies de Temnodontosaurus eran animales grandes, alcanzando algunas hasta 12 metros de longitud, de gran fuerza muscular y hábiles depredadores costeros.

facts.statement: The eyes of Temnodontosaurus could measure 20 centimeters in diameter, making them among the largest among known vertebrates.
facts.quote: Los ojos de Temnodontosaurus podían medir 20 centímetros de diámetro, haciéndolo unos de los mayores entre los vertebrados conocidos.

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus were large, very resistant swimmers capable of descending to deep zones of Jurassic seas to capture prey.
facts.quote: Eran grandes nadadores muy resistentes y podían descender hasta zonas profundas de los mares jurásicos para capturar sus presas.

facts.statement: The time range for Temnodontosaurus is the Hettangian to Toarcian, from 201.4 to 174.7 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Hettangian to Toarcian (201.4 to 174.7 million years ago)

facts.statement: A new specimen of Temnodontosaurus cf. trigonodon was described by Eggmaier & Albert in 2026 from the Lower Jurassic (Toarcian) strata of the Jurensismergel Formation in Germany.
facts.quote: A new specimen of Temnodontosaurus cf. trigonodon, providing new information on the skeletal anatomy of Temnodontosaurus and preserving evidence of pathological changes in the shoulder and jaw joints that might have been related to the animal's hunting and feeding behavior, is described from the Lower Jurassic (Toarcian) strata of the Jurensismergel Formation (Germany) by Eggmaier & Albert (2026).

facts.statement: The genus Temnodontosaurus was described by Lydekker in 1889.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Lydekker, 1889

facts.quote: its caudal fin has variously been described as either lunate or semi-lunate.
